passages.title: How To Prevent Condensation on Windows - This Old House
passages.text: Window condensation happens when there’s a significant temperature difference between the inside and outside of your home. While some condensation is normal, excessive moisture can be problematic. This guide explains the causes of window condensation, identifies its sources, and teaches how to keep your windows clear. What Causes Window Condensation? Condensation forms on windows when warm, moist air comes into contact with a cooler surface. This temperature difference causes water vapor in the air to condense into liquid droplets on the glass. In homes, this often happens when indoor humidity levels are high and outdoor temperatures are low, creating the perfect conditions for condensation to occur. Identifying the Source of Condensation There are three main sources of window condensation, all of which indicate different issues. Here’s how to recognize them. External Condensation External condensation forms on a window’s outer surface and is generally not a cause for concern. This type of condensation is similar to dew forming on grass in the morning. It typically occurs when the outside air is warmer and more humid than the window’s surface temperature. Internal Condensation Internal condensation appears on the window’s inside surface and is often a sign of excess humidity within your home.

Frost and ice on the glass During subzero stretches, which Front Range towns from Castle Rock to Fort Collins see most winters, interior condensation can freeze into frost or a band of ice along the bottom of the glass and on metal frames. When the weather warms, that ice melts all at once and runs onto the sill and wall below. Frost is the same humidity-and-cold-glass problem as liquid condensation, just more concentrated. Windows that frost regularly are good candidates for lower humidifier settings during cold snaps and for an added insulating layer. Sliding patio doors and older aluminum-framed windows are frequent trouble spots because metal frames conduct cold readily. Is it a problem? A little fogging on the coldest morning of the year that clears by mid-morning is usually minor. The concern grows when water runs down the glass, pools on sills, soaks wood frames, causes peeling paint or stains, or leads to dark spots on caulk, sills or nearby drywall. Those are signs the moisture is staying long enough to damage materials or support mold growth.

Older, less efficient windows leak more heat, which warms the outer surface and keeps it dry. No fix is needed. The dew burns off as the sun and air warm the glass. passages.text: Condensation on the inside of your windows is a real signal that indoor humidity is too high. Warm, moisture-laden air inside your home drifts against the cold glass, cools below its dew point, and the vapor condenses into the beads of water you see on the room side. Unlike dew on the outside of the glass — which is harmless weather — interior fog is worth fixing, because water left on the sill feeds mold and rots the frame. The fix is a clear sequence: ventilate the moisture at its source, lower indoor humidity to 30-50% with a dehumidifier, and warm the glass so its surface stays above the dew point. What does condensation on the inside of windows mean? It means the air inside your home holds more moisture than the cold glass can tolerate. When warm, humid indoor air meets a surface colder than its dew point, the water vapor has nowhere to go but liquid — the same physics that beads water on a cold drink in a warm room. Can I fix fog between the panes of a double-pane window myself? No. Fog trapped between panes means the insulated glass unit (IGU) seal has failed and moisture has leaked into the sealed cavity. No amount of dehumidifying will clear it — the fix is replacing the glass unit or sash, which a glass shop can often do without replacing the whole window. Will a dehumidifier stop condensation on windows? Usually, yes — if the condensation is on the room side of the glass. Lowering indoor relative humidity lowers the dew point of your air, so the glass no longer falls below it overnight. Pair the dehumidifier with a hygrometer and target 30–40% RH in freezing weather.
